topics.topic: Accepted multipart part order, cardinality, extra parts, and content type
questions: Must Registry refuse multipart requests in which the file is first, the CSRF field is repeated, another field occurs between them, or additional parts follow the file, and which occurrence is authoritative?
Is that exact two-part order an acceptance condition, and what happens to multipart requests with the file first, repeated CSRF or file parts, another part between them, or parts after the file?

What must Registry do with a multipart request whose CSRF field is missing, duplicated or not first; whose file is missing, duplicated or not second; which has extra parts; or which uses a different content type?

quotes:
The CSRF value the first part carries, the delimiter that ends the file
part, and the file part's declared length — the request's declared length
less the head it read and the closing delimiter with its final `--` and line
end, or none when the request declared none; or that the head is not of that form — no multipart content type or
boundary, a first part that is not the CSRF field, no second part that is
the file — or is longer than the imported `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES`
constant, with none of these values.

a stream that fails or ends before its
declared length is refused as `file_unreadable`, replacing nothing kept and
changing nothing of the session but the instant of its last request, which
every request carrying it moves (A13 rule 2) — and an
unreadable or malformed one is refused with its kind alone.
judgement.why: The later public API requires the CSRF field first and file second, rejects any other head, and makes trailing additional parts produce a declared-length mismatch rather than an alternative accepted upload.

topics.topic: Behavior when the file part has not begun at the multipart head limit
questions: What exactly happens when the file part has not begun after `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES`: is the upload refused, at which byte, with which refusal, and does Registry stop reading the request body?
What must Registry do when the file part has not begun by the time this many head bytes have been read, and does that refusal preserve the session's previously uploaded file?
Which bytes belong to the head, and what exactly happens if the file part has not begun when the bound is reached?

quotes:
Reads the stream up to the start of the file part's content and no further,
at most the bound; a head it refuses leaves the rest of the stream unread.
None: it reads the request's stream only.
judgement.why: The later upload-framing operation stops at the bound, refuses the head, leaves the remaining request unread, and changes no state, so an earlier upload remains kept.

topics.topic: Exact multipart framing subtracted to derive the declared file length
questions: Which exact bytes constitute the subtracted closing delimiter and tail, including the CRLF before the boundary, boundary markers, optional epilogue, and any parts after the file; and what happens when the subtraction is negative or cannot be computed?

Which exact octets constitute the head and closing delimiter, are a multipart preamble or epilogue allowed, and what happens when the declared request length is smaller than those subtracted values or disagrees with the actual framing?
Precisely which bytes count as the closing delimiter, including any CRLF, terminal boundary, epilogue or transport framing, and how is its length known before a file byte is read?

quotes:
`upload_framing.read_upload_head` reads the head alone,
  at most `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES` (8192 bytes) — the boundary from the
  content type, the CSRF part, the file part's headers — and answers
  `UploadHead`: the CSRF value, the delimiter `\r\n--<boundary>` that ends
  the file part, and the file part's declared length — the request's
  declared length less the head read and the closing delimiter with its
  final `--\r\n` — or none of them.

The declared length `_read_bounded`
  compares is the file part's, so a file of exactly 50 MB is read (A19 rule
  4's required test); a body with an epilogue after the closing delimiter
  declares more than its file, and only a file that near the limit is then
  refused early. The bytes are counted over the file part as it is read.

topics.topic: Precedence of multipart structure, CSRF, head-bound, and file-size checks
questions: After reading the first part, in what order must Registry check CSRF validity, the head bound, multipart validity, the derived declared file length, and the streamed file limit, and which refusal takes precedence when several fail?

Must Registry authenticate the CSRF value before it reads any file byte, and which refusal applies when the CSRF value is wrong and the file is oversized?

quotes:
A
head of another form gives no CSRF value, and the upload is refused at stage
(1) before any byte of the file is read.

A13 rule 7: the CSRF value is taken from the form's body, never from a URL,
and is neither checked nor kept here — `owner_sessions` checks it at the
session check. A19 rule 4 stays `migration_import`'s: no byte of the file is
read here, and the file part's stream, a `MultipartFileBody` over the same
stream and that delimiter, gives the file's bytes only as its reader asks.

A request refused at
  admission never reads its file.
judgement.why: The later operations parse the bounded head first, perform session and CSRF admission next, and only after admission let migration_import enforce declared and streamed file-size limits.

What does “never kept” prohibit, when must transient parsing buffers be discarded, and which Required tests item must show both enforcement of the head bound and disposal of the head?

When the request has no declared length, an invalid length, a length smaller than the bytes presented, or a length smaller than the multipart head plus closing delimiter, is it unreadable immediately, processed by streaming, or handled in some other specified way?

quotes:
The request's unread body stream, its content type and its declared length,
or that it declared none.

The CSRF value the first part carries, the delimiter that ends the file
part, and the file part's declared length — the request's declared length
less the head it read and the closing delimiter with its final `--` and line
end, or none when the request declared none; or that the head is not of that form — no multipart content type or
boundary, a first part that is not the CSRF field, no second part that is
the file — or is longer than the imported `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES`
